Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
The accident happened on a Tuesday afternoon in late autumn, on a stretch of highway Robert had driven a thousand times. He was returning from a client meeting in the suburbs, his mind half-occupied with fabric swatches and paint samples, when a delivery truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan at forty miles an hour. The impact crumpled the driver’s side door inward, trapping his left leg against the console, and for what felt like an eternity he hung there, suspended in the smell of gasoline and twisted metal, unable to move or breathe or cry out. By the time the paramedics cut him free, he had already begun to understand something fundamental had shifted inside him, something that had nothing to do with the cracked ribs and the hairline fracture in his femur.

In the months that followed, as his body healed and the bruises faded to yellow and then to nothing, Robert found himself living in a world that had become subtly but permanently wrong. He had always been someone who trusted his own reflexes—his work as an interior designer demanded a steady hand and a confident eye—but now he caught himself flinching at nothing, his heart hammering when he simply turned his head too quickly. The sensation was not physical pain but something deeper, a visceral certainty that his body was no longer an ally. He had come to believe that the machinery of his own flesh had betrayed him, that it could fail again without warning, and that belief made him move through his days like a man walking on ice that might crack at any step.

The triggers were everywhere, and they were merciless. A car backfiring in the parking lot of a Home Depot sent him into a cold sweat that lasted twenty minutes. The sound of tires screeching on asphalt, even from blocks away, would freeze him mid-sentence, his hand gripping whatever surface was nearest. He stopped listening to the radio in his car because he never knew when a news report would mention a collision, and he had learned the hard way that the word “accident” alone was enough to send his pulse into a gallop. His work suffered in ways he had not anticipated. He could no longer take on commercial projects that required him to drive to multiple sites in a single day, and he began turning down residential clients who lived beyond a five-mile radius from his office. His partner at the firm, a woman he had worked with for fifteen years, started covering his site visits without being asked, and Robert could see the worry in her eyes, the careful way she phrased her questions about his health.

The person he had been—the one who could walk into a room full of strangers and sell a vision, who could spend a weekend driving to antique shops across three states, who defined himself by his taste and his competence—that person had become a stranger to him. He felt hollowed out, as though the accident had not only damaged his body but had erased the blueprint of who he was. He told his therapist that he no longer recognized himself in the mirror, that the face looking back belonged to someone cautious and diminished, someone who planned escape routes from every restaurant and who could not sit with his back to a door. The idea that he might someday feel like his old self seemed not just unlikely but impossible, as though the collision had permanently rewired the circuitry of his soul into a configuration that could never be undone.

His divorce, which had been finalized two years before the accident, had left him living alone in a condo he had designed himself, and now that space had become a fortress. He had stopped hosting dinner parties. He had stopped dating. He had stopped returning calls from his grown daughter, not because he did not love her but because he could not bear the conversation, the inevitable questions about how he was doing, the effort of pretending. He spent his evenings in a leather armchair with the television muted, watching the silent flicker of images, his hands resting on his knees, his breathing shallow and deliberate. He had come to believe that any sudden movement, any loud noise, any unexpected touch might trigger a cascade he could not control.

What finally brought him to seek help was not the fear or the isolation or the professional drift, though all of those had accumulated like sediment in a river. It was a moment in the grocery store, three weeks ago, when a child dropped a jar of pasta sauce and the glass shattered on the tile floor. The sound was not loud, not really, but Robert dropped to his knees, his hands over his ears, and when a store employee touched his shoulder to ask if he was all right, he screamed. He sat in his car in the parking lot for forty minutes afterward, shaking, and he knew then that he could not go on like this. He was terrified of what he might become if he did not find a way back to himself, but he was equally terrified that the person he had been was gone forever, that the permanent damage was already done, and that no amount of talking could rebuild what the crash had broken.
